title: The pregnant woman with an acute abdomen
subtitle: Two patients, one operation, no delay

red_flags.text: Tachycardia, hypotension or a rising lactate. Pregnancy masks shock until late, and maternal hypovolaemia is fetal hypoperfusion.
Peritonism in pregnancy is often blunted: the gravid uterus lifts the abdominal wall away from the inflamed organ.
Appendicitis pain may be in the right flank or upper quadrant later in pregnancy as the appendix is displaced.
Abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding, a hard tender uterus or fetal distress: abruption, which is an obstetric emergency.
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain with hypertension: pre-eclampsia or HELLP syndrome, not gallstones.

do_now.text: From about 20 weeks, position with left lateral tilt or manual uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression, during assessment, transfer and surgery.
Involve the obstetric team at presentation, not after the decision to operate.
Do not delay an indicated operation because of the pregnancy. Delay in appendicitis and other surgical emergencies harms both mother and fetus.
Resuscitate the mother first. Oxygen, intravenous access, fluids and analgesia are the best fetal treatment.

assess.text: Gestation by dates or early scan, and fetal heart rate documented before any intervention when the fetus is viable.
Use pregnancy-adjusted interpretation of physiology and bloods: white cell count and heart rate are normally higher, blood pressure lower in the second trimester.
Consider obstetric causes alongside surgical ones: labour, abruption, pre-eclampsia, fibroid degeneration, torsion, urinary infection.

investigate.text: Ultrasound first. MRI without gadolinium is the next step when ultrasound is inconclusive.
CT is not contraindicated in pregnancy when it is needed to answer an urgent question; the dose from a single diagnostic CT is below the threshold associated with fetal harm.
Do not withhold necessary imaging with ionising radiation from a pregnant woman; explain and document the discussion.
Urinalysis, full blood count, liver function, urea and electrolytes, and blood pressure with proteinuria where pre-eclampsia is possible.

resuscitate.text: Maintain maternal oxygenation, normotension and normoglycaemia; avoid maternal hypotension during induction.
Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis: pregnancy is a prothrombotic state.
Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm birth is a risk and the gestation falls within the window the obstetric team uses.

definitive.text: Laparoscopy is safe in any trimester when indicated. Use an open entry or adjust the Veress or optical entry site to the fundal height.
Position in left lateral tilt on the table; use the lowest insufflation pressure that gives adequate view, with capnography monitored.
Appendicectomy for appendicitis in pregnancy; non-operative antibiotic treatment is not the standard in pregnancy because perforation carries a high fetal loss rate.
Fetal heart monitoring before and after surgery for a viable fetus; intra-operative monitoring is individualised and arranged with obstetrics, who must be able to intervene.

escalate.text: Theatre should be in a hospital with obstetric and neonatal cover when the fetus is viable.
Post-operatively, monitor for preterm contractions; tocolysis is not given prophylactically and is decided by obstetrics.

notes: The commonest non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy is appendicitis. The commonest error is waiting.
Ultrasound, then MRI, then CT if needed. The worst imaging choice is none.
Left lateral tilt is not a detail. Supine hypotension in the third trimester substantially reduces venous return and cardiac output.
